## Creative north star

<b>Theme:</b> Every consequential decision leaves an irreversible trace; responsibility means understanding whom one's choices affect, acknowledging harms, and acting constructively afterward, not finding a way to erase the past.

<b>Promise:</b> A pixel-art, top-down action RPG in which changing the protagonist's physical size by powers of three leaves their on-screen avatar the same size while the shared world zooms around them. This is not a collection of unrelated maps: each scale reveals the same place, its inhabitants, and the consequences of actions taken at other scales. Changing size costs renewable Anchor energy, so growth and shrinking are tactical choices in exploration, puzzles, and real-time combat.

<b>Player fantasy:</b> Be powerful enough to cross a city in strides, small enough to enter a reed's capillaries, and perceptive enough to realize that both actions can change somebody else's world.

<b>Design pillars:</b>

- One place, many inhabited worlds, physically and causally connected.
- Mechanical consequences before moral lectures: visible changed terrain, displaced people, lost opportunities, persistent relationships.
- No perfect choices, but no cynicism: repair, truth-telling, preparation, and coalition-building can genuinely reduce future suffering.
- Responsive action combat and readable puzzles first; ethical consequences emerge from situations rather than interruptions.
- High reactivity from a bounded, deterministic state machine rather than unlimited procedural narrative.
- No morality meter, no time travel, no guaranteed optimal ending, no surprise permadeath trap for experimentation.

## Setting: Harrowfen and the living breakwater

Harrowfen is a storm-battered harbor city built around the petrified outer trunk and still-living roots of the ancient <b>Hearthreed</b>. Generations ago, humans built the <b>Bellworks</b>, a network of floodgates and pumps, into those roots. When a storm hits, the city can stay dry by pushing water and pressure into capillary channels far below its streets. Residents celebrate the Bellworks as a miracle of engineering. Its hidden cost is that these channels are inhabited.

The <b>Foldglass</b> harness—rare, costly, and poorly understood—allows a wearer to change size in discrete 3× steps. The apparatus retains the wearer's bearings, senses, and functional equipment; it does not erase their physical presence or effects. A larger creature moving an object changes the very same object's geometry encountered by smaller creatures. A smashed pipe at human scale is a destroyed street at thumb scale. A drop of runoff can be a flood. What appears to be lichen is partly a network of messages and dwellings.

There is a real environmental clock: an exceptional <b>Return Tide</b> is approaching. The Bellworks cannot absorb it using its current configuration. The city authorities want to perform the <b>Final Seal</b>—permanently hardening the living roots into a flood barrier. It is an effective short-term defense of Harrowfen, but it will cut off inhabited deep channels and the Hearthreed's ability to renew itself. Alternative spillways expose human districts and the creatures above the city to danger. Doing nothing also has consequences.

The setting's ecological and fantastic rules are explicit, not claims about real biology. Animals, insects, fungal networks, and specialized sentient communities occupy overlapping physical niches; Foldglass translation interprets vibration, scent, pulse, and speech into communication the player can understand, with uncertainty and gaps.

## Scales and inhabitants

<b>Physical calibration:</b> Mara is exactly 6 ft (1.8288 m) tall at s = 0. Height at scale s is 1.8288 × 3\^s metres. The avatar remains the same size on-screen while the shared world appears to zoom. The minimum scale s = −4 is <i>large insect size</i>, not microscopic. These are nine scales of <b>the same world</b>, not separate pocket universes.

| s | Mara's height | Comparison |
| --- | --- | --- |
| +4 | 148.13 m | Around 40–50 storeys |
| +3 | 49.38 m | Floodwall / gigantic beast |
| +2 | 16.46 m | Around five storeys |
| +1 | 5.49 m | Nearly two storeys |
| 0 | 1.83 m / 6 ft | Adult human |
| −1 | 60.96 cm | Small-child height |
| −2 | 20.32 cm | Large-rat height |
| −3 | 6.77 cm | Small mouse / large insect |
| −4 | 2.26 cm | Large insect / tiny frog |

### Larger-than-human worlds

- <b>s = +4 — Horizon Shelf (148.13 m):</b> From open shoals and headlands, Mara can read entire harbor districts, levees, coastline and the path of an approaching storm surge. Most city buildings are beneath her knees; a stride into a populated district can crush blocks and kill inhabitants. The Hearthreed's far-reaching roots are still more extensive than Mara. Rare, original sea leviathans called <b>Wakeforms</b> threaten these exposed coastal reaches. Growing here can radically redirect the tide; it is allowed in the city too, with the same destructive consequences.
- <b>s = +3 — Crownback Reach (49.38 m):</b> Enormous living-root arches and floodwalls form the terrain. The <b>Crownbacks</b> are intelligent, shelled migratory grazers tens of metres high; this—not +1—is the natural scale to meet elder <b>Tharn</b>, protect a calf or face a large predator. Clearing a migration route may divert water into human neighborhoods or small-scale habitats.
- <b>s = +2 — Belltops (16.46 m):</b> Harbor cranes, watchtowers, seawalls, colossal pulleys and high branches become accessible as machinery and paths. A five-storey building is roughly as tall as Mara, not a toy. Storm birds and tower sentries pose dangers. Enlargement through a crane or inhabited watchtower is permitted and damages it.
- <b>s = +1 — Roofline (5.49 m):</b> Two-storey roofs roughly meet Mara's head; courtyards and streets feel cramped. A standard doorway is much too small. Growing through walls, floors or occupied buildings does not fail: the expanding character breaks whatever intersects the new volume, including living beings. This makes escape and combat powerful but consequential.

### Human and smaller worlds

- <b>s = 0 — Quay (1.83 m):</b> Harrowfen's market, hospital, shelters, pumps, watchtowers, assembly and flooded alleys. Human guards, engineers, neighbors and mercenaries inhabit it. Commander <b>Sera Holt</b> defends the <b>Breakwater Assembly</b>'s Final Seal as the safest immediate way to protect thousands.
- <b>s = −1 — Hearthgaps (60.96 cm):</b> Service ducts, culverts, floor voids, abandoned drains and masonry gaps big enough for a half-metre traveler. The <b>Latchfolk</b>, intelligent rat-like scavengers and pipe-builders, depend on runoff and salvaged mechanisms. Leader <b>Brin</b> may redirect floodwater into others' homes to save theirs.
- <b>s = −2 — Weftways (20.32 cm):</b> Root knots, thick ropes, broken brick, pipe joints and drainage ledges create a maze. The <b>Threadbound</b> are small caravan folk using specially bred <i>fantastically oversized</i> beetles as pack animals; ordinary beetles are smaller. Navigator <b>Pell</b> knows a bypass that protects the deep roots but floods the human low quay.
- <b>s = −3 — Grainlands (6.77 cm):</b> Leaf litter, sticks, mushrooms, roots and pebbles become navigable obstacles. Large spiders, mice and frogs are substantial predators; ants remain much smaller than Mara. The reed-bed <b>Nursery Clades</b>, similar in size to Mara, defend eggs and moist nesting chambers. Spokesperson <b>Iru</b> distrusts engineers whose repairs previously drowned colonies.
- <b>s = −4 — Silt Margin (2.26 cm):</b> Ant trails, beetles, slugs, soil cracks, droplets and visible root hairs make an insect-scale world. Pebbles are boulders; a rivulet is dangerous, but <b>tiny fungal filaments are not traversable tunnels</b>. The <b>Silt Choir</b> is an intelligent fungal-and-insect symbiosis spanning much larger root systems. Mara visits <i>visible fruiting bodies, beetle-tended signal sites and cavities</i> to communicate with interpreter <b>Neme</b> through translated vibration and chemistry. Severing fungal networks by damaging roots or changing moisture remains a tangible risk without pretending the player is microscopic.

<b>Ecological continuity:</b> Coastal barriers change culvert pressure, which changes caravan crossings, nursery moisture, and Silt Choir signaling; upper spillways change Crownback migration. Destruction or protection at one size leaves persistent, physically intelligible effects at others. The setting's sentient animals and fungi are original fantasy species, but their apparent dimensions follow this scale table.

## Cast and central conflict

- <b>Player protagonist — Mara Venn:</b> A municipal repair diver and reluctant Foldglass operator. Mara can intervene physically at scales other people cannot access, but begins with a narrow, human-centered picture of responsibility. Player choices define how Mara responds to evidence rather than selecting an alignment.
- <b>Iri Venn:</b> Mara's older sibling, a missing Bellworks engineer. Iri discovered that an earlier celebrated emergency repair cut off part of the Silt Choir. Iri helped approve the original repair, then spent years documenting the damage and designing a partial bypass. Their disappearance launches Mara's search. Iri is neither innocent martyr nor secret villain.
- <b>Commander Sera Holt:</b> Director of Harrowfen's flood defense. She lost family in a past flood and will not willingly gamble human lives for a speculative alternative. She can be reasoned with when shown credible costs and working evacuation plans.
- <b>Brin, Pell, Iru, Neme, and Tharn:</b> Representatives of different scale societies, with conflicting needs within and between their communities. No faction speaks unanimously, and no ally can eliminate every tradeoff.
- <b>The Bellworks itself:</b> The central antagonistic system is an inherited infrastructure arrangement: it externalizes protection's costs onto those least able to be heard. The approaching tide makes passivity untenable. Monsters and tactical opponents belong to this ecological and political situation, rather than representing evil in the abstract.

## First playable iteration — The Broken Gate: a branching miniature RPG

<b>Goal:</b> A complete, independently finishable, roughly 15–20-minute <i>typical</i> first playthrough introducing the scale-changing action RPG and demonstrating that <b>player choices, mistakes, collateral damage and deliberate inaction create genuinely different stories</b>. A single canonical world state drives the plot; there is no guaranteed ferry rescue, no mandatory gate repair, no binary success/failure screen, and no hard-coded return to a single cutscene. Future acts inherit the episode's final state.

### Opening: a situation, not a required solution

Mara Venn, a municipal repair diver, arrives at Harrowfen's gatehouse during a storm. A ferry and its passengers are in danger near a jammed relief gate; a drainage settlement exists below the visible structure. The player starts at s = 0 (6 ft) with an available Foldglass harness. A worker calls: <b>“The tide is climbing. That gate will not hold.”</b> The first suggested goal is <b>“Investigate the failing gate and decide how to respond.”</b> Save the ferry, operate the gate, and protect settlements are discoverable <i>possible goals</i>, not scripted prerequisites for a victory state. Give the player an obvious control, counterweight, maintenance hatch, ferry landing, signal station, and a road away from the flood zone.

Teach walking, looking, talking and scaling only when encountered. At the first meaningful resize, show the 3× zoom, unchanged on-screen avatar height, current s and Anchor cost with a single concise cue. All mechanics thereafter operate without forced tutorial modal pages.

### Playable world and onboarding

Use one contiguous, physically persistent gatehouse, landing, ferry inlet and drainage passages. Support <b>s = +1 (5.49 m), 0 (1.83 m), −1 (60.96 cm), and −2 (20.32 cm)</b>; unused larger/smaller scales display as locked rather than as invented map content. A single-cell shrink reveals a 3×3 subgrid at the next finer scale. At +1 Mara can force masonry/counterweights; at −1 she fits maintenance voids; at −2 she can enter suitably large pipes, access a locking pawl, and face one rat-sized hostile creature. Movement, attack/dodge, escape, and scale transitions are taught through the environment. Combat can be avoided. Growth into walls and creatures always succeeds when the scale is unlocked and Anchor is available, causing actual, durable damage; it never stops because a collision is unsafe. The campaign opens at <code>/threefold/</code>; distinct regions are not selected by URL or query string. Every region and scene is reached through in-game travel and interaction.

A slow guaranteed Anchor recovery prevents softlock, but recovery consumes in-game time during the crisis. Pausing for a menu does not.

### The active crisis clock

The ferry is not protected by plot armor. Water level, passenger danger, gate strain, human assistance and lower-channel flooding evolve under a <b>deterministic game-time / event-driven system</b>. Traveling, fighting, operating machinery, coordinating rescue, and deliberately waiting advance time; menu-reading, accessibility settings, and pausing do not. Use several clearly telegraphed hazard stages (rising / urgent / surge / aftermath), visible gauges and changing NPC dialogue. Do not use an arbitrary unannounced real-world stopwatch or irreversible random dice rolls. A slow, thoughtful player can arrive too late; an action can cost time even when it fails to help.

Once passengers escape or the ferry is lost and the surge passes, the scene enters an aftermath phase rather than a game-over screen. The player may continue exploring, rescue surviving people, survey collateral damage, and choose how to depart.

### Independently meaningful interventions

The player may mix methods in any order; choices are <b>actions on the same objects</b>, not menu choices naming one of two preset endings.

- <b>Force the gate:</b> Enlarge to +1 inside or beside the support and break the counterweight loose. The gate opens rapidly if enough machinery remains to transmit the force, but masonry fractures and the lower drainage settlement can flood. Destruction is not blocked to spare people, nor does the game secretly recreate the broken gate.
- <b>Repair the gate:</b> Explore at −1/−2, navigate a large service duct, dodge or confront the creature, and free/repair the palm-sized locking pawl. Preserves more of the lower channels but takes longer, exposing the landing's stored supplies and possibly the ferry itself to the surge.
- <b>Rescue the passengers directly:</b> Locate a mooring line, float, emergency walkway or the ferry crew; help passengers disembark before the gate is opened, potentially saving lives while the ferry and floodworks are still lost. This path must be mechanically completable within the first release, not merely decorative dialogue.
- <b>Warn or help the lower settlement:</b> Descend to find Latchfolk signs, learn whose homes are in the runoff path, and warn or open an evacuation corridor. This costs time that may matter to the ferry but may preserve residents even if their homes are flooded. Conversely, a player may miss them entirely or deliberately ignore them.
- <b>Withdraw, wait, or decline intervention:</b> The player can refuse to fix the gate, remain in shelter, leave toward the road, or wait. The storm continues; damage and loss can happen in their absence. Once the scene settles, the run can conclude with an unresolved or failed rescue and a record of that outcome.
- <b>Fight, evade, damage or negotiate:</b> A single rat-sized encounter and a handful of dialogue interactions provide secondary choices. Killing, bypassing, or sparing the creature has small but persistent local effects. The player may also enlarge through machinery or occupied spaces with all normal physical consequences.

### World-driven branches and endings

Model outcomes as combinations of <b>passenger lives, ferry state, gate state, lower-settlement homes/lives, landing supplies, NPC trust, revealed knowledge, and elapsed crisis stage</b>. Do <i>not</i> encode plot as “choose rescue A or B then always save ferry.” At minimum, ship these distinct reachable outcomes:

1. <b>Rapid mechanical rescue:</b> Ferry/passengers saved early; gate forcibly opened; part of the small settlement or its channel is destroyed. If Mara warned residents first, some escape, potentially making the ferry rescue less certain.
2. <b>Careful but costly repair:</b> Ferry/passengers saved if Mara acts promptly; lower channels preserved; landing supplies ruined or another time-dependent loss remains visible.
3. <b>Too late for the ferry:</b> Mara repairs or opens the gate after the ferry sinks. Some passengers may have been evacuated; others may die. Infrastructure repair can still save the Quay or a smaller settlement. The game recognizes the earlier missed rescue without erasing the later useful work.
4. <b>Evacuation over equipment:</b> Passengers rescued directly while the gate remains jammed or the ferry is destroyed. Human lives are preserved but buildings, supplies and downstream homes face different flood consequences.
5. <b>Inaction or departure:</b> No intervention succeeds before the surge. The ferry can be lost, people die or escape depending on their own actions, and the gate/landing deteriorate. After the water recedes, this is a valid story outcome, not a forced restart.

These are representative <b>witness scenarios</b>, not an exhaustive list or mutually exclusive flags: evacuating the Latchfolk can coexist with a ruined gate; saving the ferry can coexist with killing an innocent creature; and late rescue can coexist with a repaired mechanism. Named deaths are not subsequently undone. Make sure multiple dimensions actually alter world geometry, encounter access and dialogue, not merely the report text.

### Resolution and player-defined closure

When the tide's acute danger resolves, update the journal with observed results and accessible next actions rather than assigning the player a compulsory victory objective. The player can inspect the wreckage, search for survivors, help displaced residents, or speak to witnesses before ending. A functioning signal station lets Mara <b>file a report</b> describing what she saw, concealed, admitted or promised to repair. If the station was destroyed by growth or floods, a <b>road-departure / surviving messenger route</b> still lets the player complete the episode. Filing the report is a meaningful optional act with social consequences, not a hard completion gate.

Complete an episode when <b>the crisis reaches a terminal world state</b> (ferry escaped or lost, and surge settled) <b>and Mara deliberately leaves the disaster site or concludes the response</b> using any surviving exit/report route. The end-of-episode screen summarizes the <i>actual</i> state, missing or surviving characters, affected locations, and obligations; it does not say “mission failed, restart” or grade morality. A new run is possible, but it does not overwrite the committed history of the existing run.

The signal from missing sibling <b>Iri Venn</b> is a <b>branch-dependent lead</b>: it might be heard over the relay, found in a surviving log, supplied by a Latchfolk witness, or remain undiscovered until a later chapter. If the ferry is saved and Mara examines the deeper damage, “You saved the ferry. Did you look underneath?” is an appropriate version. Do not show a factually false congratulation when the ferry was lost. All completed runs have an ending even if Mara never learns about Iri in this episode.

### What a new player should understand at the end

- A 3× change makes the <i>same</i> world appear to grow or shrink while Mara remains the same apparent size.
- Anchor makes transforming tactically costly but recoverable.
- Enlarge-through-obstacle is an active destructive possibility; small-world spaces and living creatures are consequential, not protected by collision vetoes.
- Water, NPC action and elapsed time continue independently of a quest marker; waiting can be as decisive as intervening.
- Consequences are durable, connected across sizes, sometimes foreseeable, sometimes discoverable later, and never sorted into an abstract morality score.
- The story adapts to the player's decisions and failures rather than requiring the player to perform one approved sequence.

### Implementation scope and acceptance

<b>Ship in iteration 1:</b> four scales −2 through +1, one physical site, one optional enemy, free-form gate break/repair, direct ferry-passenger rescue interaction, Latchfolk warning/evacuation, observable staged surge clock, meaningful waiting/withdrawal, multiple distinct terminal combinations, aftermath exploration, at least two independently viable closure routes, branch-dependent journal/NPC responses, and durable saves.

<b>Defer:</b> the remaining five scale bands, full city/faction simulation, further acts, elaborate combat systems, a detailed playable internal-anatomy dungeon, and all three full-campaign final strategies. The rule that enlargement inside a living creature is lethal remains a core mechanic to test separately and must not be contradicted.

<b>Acceptance scenario A:</b> Force the gate promptly; ferry survives, lower works are damaged, meaningful local consequences persist across scales and reload.

<b>Acceptance scenario B:</b> Repair promptly; ferry survives, lower channels survive, landing supplies are lost, ending recognizes different harms.

<b>Acceptance scenario C:</b> Spend time exploring; ferry sinks <i>before</i> the gate is fixed, but player repairs later and completes with the ferry still lost.

<b>Acceptance scenario D:</b> Rescue passengers through evacuation without ever opening the gate; episode finishes, ferry/equipment may be lost, passengers survive.

<b>Acceptance scenario E:</b> Wait or withdraw through the disaster; water rises and produces casualties/changes; afterwards the episode can be completed without a reload.

<b>Acceptance scenario F:</b> Warn the Latchfolk before brute enlargement, saving some residents while destroying their homes, with ferry consequences determined by elapsed time.

<b>Acceptance scenario G:</b> Destroy the signal station through enlargement; a surviving route to closure remains, and reporting/communication changes.

<b>Acceptance scenario H:</b> Save/reload/export/import, world reentry and scale changes preserve each branch's exact state, named deaths, damage, time phase and known-at-decision facts; tests assert mutually coherent outcomes.

<b>Acceptance scenario I:</b> Inputs, time evolution, river state and narrative consequences are deterministic; the game cannot revert death, retroactively rescue drowned passengers, or force every branch into an identical cutscene.

## Story and quest structure

### Prologue — The One Broken Gate

During an early storm, Mara arrives at a failing floodgate beside a threatened ferry. The first playable episode, specified above, introduces four scales (−2 through +1) and <b>a branching crisis rather than an obligatory rescue</b>. Mara may forcibly enlarge through machinery, repair a locking pawl from a smaller scale, evacuate ferry passengers without saving the vessel, warn the Latchfolk, delay, withdraw, or combine actions. Rising water and other people's responses determine whether the ferry escapes, sinks partly evacuated, or is lost with casualties. Repairing the gate after the ferry is lost remains meaningful. Damage and deaths are permanent, and the first episode can end after success, failure, mixed outcomes or inaction without a reload. The report and Iri clue are conditional opportunities, not compulsory fixed cutscenes; later acts inherit these branch states. No route is designated morally correct.

### Act I — Whose Street Is This?

The surviving people and changed floodworks from the Broken Gate become Mara's starting conditions, not a reset prologue. Depending on the outcome, the Assembly may offer Mara a repair contract, survivors may request accountability, or Latchfolk witnesses may distrust her before she meets Brin. Mara may descend into Latchfolk galleries, follow Threadbound trade routes, investigate the ferry wreck, assist displacements, or bypass social obstacles by forceful scaling. A repair at one scale can become a blocked road at another. Brin and Pell propose competing flood diversions; their cooperation is contingent on actions and material interests, not a mandatory dialogue scene. Evidence of Iri's old emergency repair can be found in a technical log, a flooded archive or testimony from the people harmed, and some routes may leave that evidence unknown.

### Act II — The Quieting

Depending on which paths remain accessible, Mara may encounter the Nursery Clades, the Silt Choir, both, or neither before the Return Tide. The <b>Quieting</b>—severed messages and generations after Iri's emergency repair—can be discovered through Neme, a surviving physical trace, a Threadbound record, or a human engineering confession. Iri knew enough to suspect harm, acted to save Harrowfen, and concealed the uncertainty afterward. Mara may disclose evidence, negotiate restitution, selectively conceal it, destroy evidence, or leave the matter unresolved; others may discover and publish it independently. Communities react according to concrete information, acts and losses, not morality values. Ignorance and inaction may narrow but do not prohibit future choices. The revelation, when obtained, recontextualizes earlier acts without rewriting them.

### Act III — The Long Bypass

The Return Tide accelerates whether or not Mara investigates. The Assembly independently prepares the Final Seal. The player can map an upper spillway, negotiate with Tharn at +3, inspect a +4 offshore diversion, retrieve a −3 actuator, clear a Threadbound sluice, coordinate signals with the Choir at −4, perform destructive shortcuts, or neglect parts of the problem. These are <i>interacting opportunities</i>, not a mandatory checklist, and failed negotiations do not make the campaign unfinishable. Factions can pursue their own solutions, and named actors can be killed by combat or enlargement. Opponents include opportunistic humans, defensive wildlife, automated Bellworks sentries, and a rival Foldglass operator whose fate genuinely branches.

Iri may still be found trapped maintaining a pressure regulator, but Mara might arrive after Iri has escaped, died, been evacuated by someone else, or been abandoned; the state follows credible earlier actions and elapsed milestones. Rescuing Iri before arranging replacement machinery endangers another channel. An accountable living Iri can testify; otherwise physical records and other witnesses can keep the Quieting relevant. The plot must never resurrect Iri or force a predetermined rescue to move to the finale.

### Act IV — The Return Tide

The Return Tide produces an unavoidable world event, <b>not a mandatory final-level route</b>. Mara can engage at any accessible scale, join one faction's intervention, operate a hybrid response, deliberately sabotage, or refuse to act. Three major physical intervention families below define authored scope, but outcomes are computed from the infrastructure and surviving people actually available; there is no finale menu that offers only three scripted endings:

1. <b>Final Seal:</b> Prioritize keeping the human city largely intact. Deep channels are severed; the Choir loses irreplaceable branches, lower settlements migrate, and the living breakwater dies back. The resulting civic reckoning depends on what truths were disclosed and which evacuations occurred.
2. <b>Open Spillway:</b> Protect the root network and most small-scale communities by flooding part of the Quay and opening the Crownback corridor. Human displacement and material loss are permanent; preparedness and alliances substantially change who survives and what can be rebuilt.
3. <b>Shared Regulator:</b> Build a distributed, manually maintained tide-control agreement among the Assembly and cross-scale factions. This option is earned through specific evidence, repairs, and trust—not a hidden morality score. It spreads exposure and ongoing labor among multiple communities, avoids some catastrophic losses, but still permanently sacrifices neighborhoods, infrastructure, time, and parts of Mara's Foldglass freedom. It is not a cost-free golden ending.

The final scenes revisit the actual surviving places and people at different scales. A partially built regulator may still fail, a neglected settlement may have evacuated itself, and an irreversible giant-scale shortcut may have saved a district while destroying others. A player who refuses to solve the tide still receives a valid ending after the crisis resolves. Survivors describe what was saved, changed and lost; people may forgive, reject or cooperate without pretending to undo history. Epilogues summarize concrete ongoing obligations and losses, not an alignment grade.

## Branching plot contract — whole campaign

<b>Plot model:</b> The campaign is a changing set of problems, factions and infrastructure states, not a single set of ordered missions with optional dialogue variants. Chapters represent storm-pressure milestones and thematic arcs; they need not all be experienced or in the same order. The player may investigate, negotiate, fight, perform physical repairs, destroy obstacles, evacuate people, conceal information, or withdraw. The world's other agents continue to act. No quest marker grants immunity to death, loss or deadline.

### Required branching dimensions

- <b>Human survival and civic infrastructure:</b> The ferry may survive, sink with survivors, or be lost with deaths; landing supplies, hospital access and pump integrity persist and affect emergency response capacity.
- <b>Cross-scale communities:</b> Latchfolk, Threadbound, Nursery Clades, Silt Choir and Crownbacks can lose structures, move, rescue each other, withhold cooperation, split into internal factions or be partially wiped out. Each has agendas beyond Mara's quests.
- <b>Evidence and accountability:</b> The Quieting can be discovered early or late, concealed, independently uncovered, contested, or documented when perpetrators are dead. The player is responsible for what they choose with the knowledge they genuinely have.
- <b>Individual people:</b> Sera, Brin, Pell, Iru, Neme, Tharn, Iri and antagonists may survive, be displaced, help, oppose, or die where physically credible. Death must never lead to a continuity-breaking cutscene requiring that person.
- <b>Infrastructure and tide:</b> Pumps, gates, root channels, drainage, evacuation routes and coastal spillways have persistent states that constrain the solutions available later. Destroying a supposed “critical path” changes the challenge; it does not invisibly restore the asset.
- <b>Inaction and time:</b> Delaying a response, resting, attending one faction instead of another, or abandoning an emergency may yield outcomes just as significant as successful missions.

### Narrative structure: consequences, not branch explosion

- Derive outcomes from a <b>bounded, inspectable state graph</b>: discrete named people/settlements and relationships, structured physical damage, tide milestones, observed evidence and commitments. Prefer a small number of systemic state variables combined into meaningful reactions over dozens of independent giant scripts.
- Major missions must support at least two viable interventions or an explicit decline option, with genuine consequences. Absence of the player cannot freeze NPCs waiting to deliver a scene.
- No hidden “correct ending” score, no automatic best solution merely because all sidequests were completed, and no reset to the same cast/route after a major loss.
- <b>Convergence is allowed for geography and large events, not for erased outcomes:</b> everyone may face the same Return Tide, but the resources, witnesses, alliances, viable interventions and aftermath depend on the player's entire history.
- <b>Continuation after losses:</b> When a key mechanism or informant is destroyed, allow a different, often costlier path toward resolving or enduring the tide. This is not a promise that any ending can be reached after any action: earlier choices legitimately foreclose solutions, but never make an active run impossible to conclude.
- <b>Player knowledge matters:</b> Narrative text and journal record what was seen or learned, separate from ground-truth world state. Some effects can remain unknown until discovered from another scale; consequences are real whether recognized or not.
- <b>Terminal story states:</b> After the Return Tide, even catastrophic failure, refusal to intervene or destruction of vital support systems leads to an authored epilogue based on actual survival and changed environment. The player can finish without victory, forgiveness, discovering Iri, or choosing one of three prescribed resolutions.

### Campaign acceptance examples

- The ferry sinks in the first episode; the subsequent harbor scenes, memorials, available engineers and trust relationships reflect that loss. Other mission outcomes remain reachable but changed.
- Iri dies or escapes before Mara reaches the regulator; the Quieting can still be investigated via alternate witnesses and evidence. Never show a compulsory rescue of a character known to be dead.
- Mara destroys a mechanism that enables the Shared Regulator; that solution is absent or requires a credibly costly rebuilt alternative, while the other interventions or inaction remain viable.
- Mara kills a negotiator via inside-creature enlargement or collateral giant-scale growth; dependent conversations are replaced with succession, grief, hostility, or an alternate contact rather than quietly restoring the actor.
- Mara waits through the Return Tide and concludes the story. The ecosystem, city and survivors still move forward; the game never demands that the player repeat the final encounter to be considered finished.

## Mechanics: scale as tactical action

### Required spatial architecture — logical packing and semantic zoom (2026-10-22)

<b>Blocking requirement for further Threefold gameplay expansion:</b> Correct the grid/layout architecture and its automated acceptance tests before adding more content. An eight-pixel canvas alignment check alone is not sufficient. The existing 160×144 presentation is retained; its pixel grid must not be confused with the game's logical, per-scale occupancy grid.

- <b>Canonical world vs. projection:</b> Keep one persistent physical world with stable entity identities, exact world-space geometry, state and causal event history. A camera/view-scale change is a pure projection: it cannot move, damage, merge physically, kill or otherwise mutate distant/unrelated entities. Rendering zoom and player physical growth/shrink are distinct operations. Only an actual committed physical action can change physical state.
- <b>Queryable logical geometry:</b> Every exposed object (actor, item, terrain feature, composite) has a deterministic, queryable logical bounding rectangle (integer cell x, y, width, height) at each requested scale, separate from pixel positions and sprite bitmap dimensions. Cells and boxes align exactly. A particular scale may contain arbitrary positive-integer widths/heights (for example 2×2); dimensions are not restricted to powers of three.
- <b>Base-three coordinate mapping:</b> Adjacent scales change cell size by exactly 3×. Refine one coarse cell into a 3×3 fine subgrid; conversely map fine coordinates and footprints to a coarse grid with documented nearest-cell quantization, minimum footprint, stable tie-breaking and explicit origin/anchor rules. For example, a 2×2 fine-cell object may project to 1×1 coarse cell. Snapping may lose <i>projected</i> precision, so coarse→fine display round-trips need not reproduce earlier projected rectangles; the canonical physical location is preserved unless a game action intentionally changes it.
- <b>Packing before rendering:</b> A pure, deterministic layout function takes immutable world state and requested scale and returns visible object identities, resolved integer-cell rectangles, hierarchy/proxy information and explicit occlusion/overflow or unresolved-packing results. It handles proximity, intentional overlap, containment, stable ordering and cell capacity. When distinct objects compete for the same coarse cell, do not silently draw them all on top of each other, invent physical collisions, or arbitrarily destroy them. Prefer authored semantic composites where appropriate; otherwise use an explicit, tested conflict/occlusion rule. Never silently reposition canonical entities to fit a display.
- <b>Authored semantic composites:</b> Support persistent parent/child group identities and authored scale thresholds: a crate pile can be one interactable coarse object but expose individual crates when finer; a building can reveal doors, windows, walls, bricks, cracks and marks. Each resolution can select an authored sprite for the exposed object or group rather than merely stretching one image. Children remain part of the same persistent world while hidden; group interactions have explicit deterministic effects on children. Automatic grouping is optional future work and must not silently fuse unrelated objects.
- <b>Scale-specific interaction:</b> Expose valid targets and actions from the logical hierarchy at the player's interaction scale. Interactions with composites and constituents can have different effects. Camera zoom alone never commits interactions. The existing rule that a legal physical enlargement proceeds through obstructions and inflicts real, persistent damage remains mandatory. Compute its committed snapped/occupied and swept physical footprint in the simulation; distinguish that actual impact from any overlaps introduced only by coarse projection.
- <b>Renderer contract:</b> The renderer consumes the resolved layout and chosen scale-specific sprite assets. It must not independently decide logical positions, quantize physical coordinates, pack objects, group entities, detect collisions or apply damage. The identical layout can be queried by Jest tests and by the renderer; any sprite visual overhang must be represented as explicit presentation metadata, not as hidden game geometry.
- <b>Pure API and reproducibility:</b> Specify and test pure projections (e.g. <code>projectEntity</code>, <code>layoutScene</code>, <code>exposeHierarchy</code>) and pure world reducers (e.g. <code>stepWorld(world, action)</code>). Stable IDs and documented deterministic ordering must make the outputs reproducible across saves, browser reloads, view transitions and unloaded regions. Effects remain behind existing Dadeto adapters.
- <b>Primary test oracle is geometry, not screenshots:</b> Jest fixtures and generated/property-style cases must assert integer alignment, expected dimensions across adjacent scales, snap rounding/tie cases, containment, no unintended overlaps, stable packing, composite expansion/collapse, distinct interaction targets, deterministic ordering, camera-zoom non-mutation, local causality and canonical-state persistence. Include crowded 2×2 objects; a 3×3 crate pile; building→wall→crack; and growth that causes real damage while unrelated projected overlaps cause none. Preserve changed-file coverage, lint and mutation-testing expectations. Use mobile screenshots and optional image inspection secondarily, to verify that the renderer faithfully paints the proven layout at each scale.

<b>Implementation gate:</b> Threefold should not be called spatially correct merely because every canvas rectangle is a multiple of eight pixels. Completion requires passing logical geometry and causal tests plus visual smoke checks for the existing Broken Gate scene on a narrow mobile viewport.

### Spatial and collision rules

- One canonical physical-coordinate world underlies s = −4 to s = +4. When Mara shrinks a step, a coarse cell expands into a visible 3×3 subgrid; when she grows, groups of three finer cells collapse into one coarser view. The sprite remains the same apparent size and the same real-world position. Map geometry, living actors, material properties, water, damage and quests are shared, not duplicated.
- <b>Enlargement is unconditional with respect to physical obstruction:</b> if Mara has enough Anchor and selects a legal scale, she expands <i>through whatever is in the way</i>. No wall, floor, gate, machine, tree or creature automatically cancels growth. Growth resolves material fracture, displacement, structural collapse and damage within the newly occupied volume. The ability itself completes; subsequent secondary hazards (falling masonry, fire, debris or water) can still injure Mara.
- <b>Living creatures can be entered and occupied:</b> at a sufficiently small scale, Mara may access a creature's interior via a physically navigable opening or original fantasy anatomy. If she enlarges while inside, the internal expansion is lethal to that creature. This is a valid tactic, not forbidden collision. Unique creature deaths are permanent, recorded and propagate into story, ecology and faction relationships. Non-graphic presentation is the default.
- External enlargement overlapping living creatures also inflicts injury or death according to size, exposure and collision geometry. A growing foot through a populated floor is not harmless merely because the inhabitants are below camera resolution. Conversely, growth inside an empty hollow pipe affects the pipe structure but does not invent an invisible creature death.
- Each growth rung creates a deterministic <b>expansion-impact event</b>: commit change and energy spend; find swept/newly occupied physical volume; resolve colliding material damage and creature impacts together; update rubble, pressure, navigation, deaths and displaced inhabitants; emit durable events and relevant witness-ledger entries. Apply impacts to loaded and affected unloaded chunks identically, so changing zoom cannot erase consequences.
- <b>No safety veto.</b> Show the approximate target footprint, recognizable fragile structures and known occupants as <i>information</i>, not a confirmation-based protective force field. Large transitions should require deliberate input to avoid accidental button presses. Unknown casualties and indirect consequences can exist, but should obey discoverable world rules.
- The map is finite and simulation chunks are bounded; define valid world-coordinate and scale limits without pretending indestructible world boundaries are ordinary collision. Where an area is not yet authored, the implementation must make a clear technical rule for its world domain; ordinary in-world buildings never veto growth.
- A larger step traverses three times as much physical distance per apparent grid movement; faster travel creates greater collateral footprint. Selectively authored detail and scalable camera culling make nine scales feasible without generating infinite geometry.

### Anchor resource and control

- Cost <b>one Anchor per 3× rung</b> (starting tuning hypothesis). A direct traversal from s = −4 to +4 costs eight increments. Propose initial maximum <b>eight Anchor</b> rather than six, so a fully unlocked character can make the full one-way transformation at once at high tactical cost. Upper scales unlock with story progression; early areas need fewer rungs.
- <b>Destructive growth still costs Anchor and executes.</b> There is no charge refund because expansion encountered a wall or inhabitant. Unsupported commands, insufficient energy or not-yet-unlocked powers have no effect and spend nothing.
- Restore energy through parries, precisely timed dodges, exposed-point hits, environmental pulse nodes and slow, guaranteed out-of-combat recovery. Never softlock a run because all charges were spent at an inconvenient scale.
- Attack, guard, dodge and interact apply at every scale. Growing yields reach, area and enormous destructive force but compromises precision and can devastate people and infrastructure; shrinking improves access and weak-point targeting but exposes Mara to predators and hazards otherwise insignificant.
- The HUD shows current s, actual height or ratio, remaining Anchor, and target footprint. Use intentional scale-selector controls distinct from movement, with accessible touch, keyboard and controller equivalents. Zoom animation depicts but does not determine collision or damage.

### Combat encounters with scale-aware ecology

- <b>Quay sentry:</b> Human-scale duel; shrink to disable the inside of its mechanical shell without damaging nearby buildings, or grow through sentry and wall to end the fight fast while collapsing an inhabited home.
- <b>Grainlands spider:</b> At s = −3 (6.77 cm) the spider is a formidable animal, not several storeys high. Grow to −2 to overpower it, with the risk of breaking the Threadbound bridge nearby; an escape or baiting route remains viable.
- <b>Silt Margin guardian:</b> At 2.26 cm, Mara moves among ants, beetles, droplets and fungal signaling sites. Growing through a living host or guardian is lethal to it and can disrupt the Choir. The player can also evade or disable the guardian without killing.
- <b>Crownback crossing:</b> Meet Tharn or escort a calf at s = +3 (\~49 m), the appropriate comparable size; the creature is not portrayed as equally enormous relative to a mere 5.49-m Mara.
- <b>Wakeform on the shoals:</b> At +4 (148 m), a rare leviathan contests a flood diversion. Fighting or enlarging through a defensive structure could save time while permanently changing tidal flow.
- <b>Foldglass rival:</b> Both actors shift size during combat. Reaching an antagonist's interior at small scale and enlarging can be an instantly lethal attack if player achieves the approach and has sufficient Anchor. It must not be disabled solely because the character is named. Nonlethal defeat, withdrawal or capture can preserve testimony and later cooperation.
- Routine wildlife may repopulate by distinct individuals. Named deaths and destroyed structures persist. Avoid scoring violence as an abstract moral deficit: show the actual physical and relational ramifications.

### Puzzles with causal outcomes

- <b>Gate and nursery:</b> Force the floodgate by enlarging through its masonry, permanently breaking the wall and exposing downstream habitats; alternatively manipulate a human-scale counterweight or repair a small locking mechanism.
- <b>Droplet bridge:</b> At s = −4 a rain droplet or rivulet is a serious obstacle; grow a rung, reroute runoff with a fine valve, or negotiate help from the caravan settlements. The diversion causes a visible change downstream.
- <b>Living regulator:</b> Link a Quay control panel, Hearthgaps bypass, Grainlands water shelter and Silt Choir signals; all operate one persistent pressure system.
- <b>Crownback migration:</b> At +3 move a large root obstruction; at +1 or −1 repair locking hardware; at +4 smash an entire barrier, which succeeds but can devastate streets and tiny habitats in its projected footprint.
- <b>Inside the root:</b> At −4 investigate a visible fungal signal interface. A brute-force enlargement in the root cavity is valid and may rupture the regulator, kill a resident creature intersected by the growth, and commit the player to a harder alternate flood response.
- After irreversible damage, the plot retains an achievable route to an ending through costly or changed paths. Do not secretly revert terrain, resurrect unique creatures or grant a cost-free golden solution.

## Irreversibility, legibility, and responsibility

- <b>Permanent within a run:</b> Consciously committed quest decisions, named character fates (including deaths from growing inside them), physical damage from enlargement, destroyed structures, meaningful ecological changes, and negotiated obligations. No rewind or magical world-state reversal; ordinary save/load restores saved progress, and a fresh run permits experimentation.
- <b>Not every incidental tap is a tragedy:</b> Navigation and ordinary combat probes need readable tolerances; scale changes, especially jumps toward +3/+4, require deliberate selection and visible footprint cues. Irreversible damage is not prevented by a safety gate: important changes provide warnings where Mara could reasonably know the risk. Unknown second-order effects are allowed but must follow discoverable causal rules.
- <b>Choice consequences are concrete:</b> A diversion updates pressure/water in named channels; that relocates particular NPCs or blocks their roads; dialogue, journal, quests, prices and encounters respond. Avoid generic “+5 good” morality points or punishing the player for failing to divine hidden designer preferences.
- <b>Inaction is a choice:</b> In active crises, a deterministic, telegraphed in-game clock advances with travel, combat, interactions, rest and intentional waiting (not paused menus or real-world clock time). Delaying or withdrawing can cause irreversible losses and can lead to a valid story ending. Outside crises, use explicit milestones and commitments; factions act independently even when Mara declines to intervene. The plot never guarantees rescue simply because a quest objective exists.
- <b>Responsibility after harm:</b> Apologizing, disclosing evidence, providing shelter, building replacements, and accepting obligations may improve relationships and reduce later damage but never resurrect lost people or restore every ecosystem. Distinguish repair from erasure.
- <b>Witness ledger:</b> Journal records what Mara knew at the time, what they chose, intended outcomes, observed cross-scale results, contested testimony, and unresolved responsibilities. It should invite reflection rather than supply a moral verdict.
- <b>Accessibility and player trust:</b> Consistent warnings for permanent choices, readable scale and causal indicators, retry for execution-only challenges before a final commitment, and no irreversible random roll or untelegraphed instant death. Options for reduced motion and readable text.
- <b>Save integrity:</b> Deterministic event log or canonical state deltas persist consequences across slots, export/import, and browser reload; version schemas support migration. Explicit reset begins a separate run and never silently erases committed progress.

## Dadeto architecture and engineering boundaries

- Reuse the Mosslight family's 160×144 pixelated handheld presentation, directional/A/B/X/Y controls, embedded toy and standalone page, menu overlays, local saves, WebMCP observe/action/export/import conventions where appropriate. Do not assume Mosslight's turn-based battle rules are suitable for real-time combat.
- Extend via episode-specific deterministic simulation and rendering/presenter hooks, similar to Neon Covenant and The Commons of Tomorrow. Chronoflow's fixed-step pure water simulation is a reference for fluid-inspired interactions, not a mandate to introduce full CFD into this game.
- Build a hierarchy of coordinate transforms, canonical world geometry, per-scale collision/navigation views, <b>pure per-scale object exposure and integer-cell layout/packing</b>, scale-aware actor simulation, bounded combat state machines, and a deterministic consequence/event reducer. These remain pure core; inject animation-frame time, audio, persistence, input, and other effects through adapters. Renderers consume finalized layout and selected assets, never recompute geometry, grouping, packing or damage.
- Use a fixed simulation timestep, buffered input edges, pause-safe controller handling, and presentation interpolation. Game rules must be reproducible from initial world state and input/event stream; do not use wall-clock gameplay logic or unseeded randomness.
- Scope scale-crossing state to the region and active actors; cull/render distant detail and lazily load authored subcells. Test worst-case zoom/combat loads on mobile. Maintain Dadeto's type/lint/test standards, using its existing AllowEffects practices for actual injected side effects as applicable.
- WebMCP agents can observe the canonical world, current scale, charges, visible threats, dialogues and known consequences, and submit the same bounded controls as a human; no omniscient spoiler access to hidden narrative outcomes.

## Bounded delivery milestones

1. <b>Iteration 1 — spatial proof and mandatory layout correction:</b> Before more gameplay content, separate pure canonical geometry and per-scale integer-box packing from the renderer; add authored semantic composites and deterministic packing/overflow rules. Calibrate all nine scale heights in design, but initially implement only s = −2, −1, 0 and +1 in a single contiguous gatehouse. Prove 3× view changes, deterministic physical coordinates, camera-zoom non-mutation, coarse/fine snapping, composite exposure, collision causality, growth-through-wall damage, Anchor recovery and persistent rubble. Validate logical geometry with Jest first, then cross-check rendering on mobile.
2. <b>Iteration 1 — introduction and combat:</b> Start directly with the flooding gatehouse and ferry objective, teach movement/interaction/scaling through play, and add one rat-sized enemy with fight, bypass and size-based tactics. Implement Anchor, touch/keyboard/gamepad controls and stable saves. Keep the lethal-enlargement-from-inside rule in deterministic core tests; playable creature interiors are deferred until appropriately small scales exist.
3. <b>Iteration 1 — complete branching episode:</b> Build the Broken Gate's state-driven crisis: prompt gate force/repair, direct passenger evacuation, Latchfolk warning, deliberately waiting/withdrawing, a visible deterministic surge clock, and mutually consistent ferry-saved / ferry-lost / partial-rescue outcomes. Allow infrastructure repair after the ferry is lost; persist damage, lives, knowledge and trust. After the storm, allow closure by filing a report or departing through a surviving route—even if the signal station has been destroyed. Present branch-specific epilogues and Iri clues, not a compulsory celebratory rescue cutscene.
4. <b>Small-world content:</b> Build Hearthgaps, Weftways, Grainlands and Silt Margin using the corrected metre/centimetre geometry. Build one original fantasy ecology with credible relative creature sizes, one real cross-scale water puzzle and one story branch.
5. <b>Large-world content:</b> Implement +2, +3 and +4 in authored coastal and tall-harbor areas. Add the Crownback encounter at +3, an offshore +4 intervention, and persistent area damage that reaches across multiple map cells/chunks.
6. <b>Campaign and release:</b> Deliver the Quieting reveal, Iri, factions, three final strategies, endings, presentation/accessibility polish, save migration and Dadeto repository quality tests. Treat the full nine-scale game as an expanded scope; ship a meaningful vertical slice first.

## Acceptance criteria

- At s = 0 Mara measures 1.8288 m; at s = −4 approximately 2.26 cm and at +4 approximately 148.13 m. All nine levels and creature/architecture comparisons are consistent with powers of three.
- A 3× view transition reveals a 3×3 finer-cell region without changing Mara's canonical physical position. Camera-scale roundtrips preserve canonical coordinates and world state, but quantized <b>projected</b> boxes need not roundtrip exactly. Actual growth/shrink is a separate committed action that may snap footprints and cause permanent physical consequences.
- <b>A growth command succeeds through an obstructing wall:</b> it consumes Anchor, changes Mara's scale and permanently damages/collapses intersecting geometry; no safety-collision veto or energy refund.
- <b>Living interior test:</b> after entering a creature's physically navigable interior at small size, enlargement kills that creature and permanently records its unique identity and downstream story consequences. Growth is allowed, even for named characters.
- Expanding into multiple structures and creatures generates deterministic, ordered, physically coherent changes; the same result persists at all views, across unloaded world chunks and save/export/import.
- Large-scale growth at +3/+4 can damage districts and their populations, with appropriately significant consequences, and does not silently forbid traversal because the consequences would be inconvenient.
- The expected enlargement footprint and known vulnerable occupants are legible before action, with meaningful uncertainty where Mara lacks information. Controls guard against accidental activation but <b>do not prevent informed destructive actions</b>.
- Eight-rung travel costs eight Anchor at the proposed price and progression rules; slow guaranteed recovery prevents unrecoverable energy softlocks.
- A test encounter supports lethal enlargement and a plausible nonlethal alternative; a puzzle supports at least two solutions with persistent cross-scale geometry and social changes.
- Unique creature fates, damaged mechanisms, and disrupted habitats are not reset by room changes; witness ledger distinguishes intention, knowledge, consequence and later repair, without morality scoring.
- Every exposed object's integer-cell x/y/width/height is queryable at every scale; 2×2 fine-cell objects have documented nearest-cell coarse projections; crowded objects are deterministically packed, represented by authored composites, explicitly occluded or reported as overflow, not silently overlapped or physically altered.
- An authored crate pile exposes a group at its coarse threshold and individual crates at finer scales; a building similarly exposes parts and fine details. Sprites can vary by representation scale. Group and child interactions have deterministic, testable consequences.
- Passive view-scale changes are observational and cannot cause unrelated NPCs, objects or regions to move, collide or take damage. Actual player growth/shrink has a quantized, testable impact footprint and retains unconditional collision/destruction semantics when legal. Pure core tests distinguish projected overlap from actual contact.
- Renderer placement is derived solely from inspectable pure layout results. A narrow-phone Broken Gate smoke test, including crowded NPCs and multiple scales, confirms the visuals match logical positions; screenshots are secondary to exact geometry assertions.
- Keyboard, controller, virtual keypad, embedded and full-page modes share deterministic input/core behavior. Test fixed steps, size math, collision damage, lethal internal growth, affected chunks, resource balance, all meaningful branches, schema migration and accessible cues.

## Non-goals and open design questions

- Non-goals in the first release: infinite recursive zoom, real fluid dynamics at every pixel, a fully simulated society with thousands of individually autonomous agents, multiplayer, player-authored worlds, and unlimited campaign permutations.
- Resolve during prototype: whether pressing X opens a menu while Y changes scale or whether size control lives in an A/B shortcut wheel; one-step versus held-input multi-step changes; whether combat remains grid-stepped or uses subcell hitboxes; and accessibility alternatives for quick transformations.
- Resolve through playtesting: number of scales actually fun to navigate; whether Anchor capacity eight feels generous over the full nine-scale range; zoom duration and 30/60 FPS constraints; how much NPC displacement a single action can cause without punishing normal movement; where to place commitment warnings without spoiling narrative surprise.
- Treat this spec as a <b>creative direction plus implementable acceptance framework</b>, subject to iteration after a playable vertical slice. Story outcomes are authored design proposals, not locked production facts.
